extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and scholars interested in ethics, moral philosophy, and social theory (readers of Popular Science Monthly / reviewers of ethical systems)
extracted.subtask_description: Critically evaluating a systematic moral theory (here, Spencer's 'Data of Ethics') for its coherence, empirical adequacy, motivational force, and practical applicability to human life and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduciveness to vitality (pleasures list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral value of actions is judged by a list of pleasures denoting the conduciveness of the action to vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spencer's criterion: pleasures that indicate conduciveness to vitality. Reviewer questions whether absence of higher moral striving (e.g., 'no moral effort, no moral conflict') makes a state lower; example discussion of whether lack of moral struggle implies moral inferiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary/perfection characteristics (adjustment, definiteness, exactness, heterogeneity, complexity, multiformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral worth is assessed by characteristics derived from 'perfection of evolution' such as 'adjustment of an action to an end,' 'definiteness,' 'exactness,' 'heterogeneity,' 'complexity,' 'multiformity,' and the subordination of immediate to remote objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes these attributes can be displayed in evil actors (Napoleon, Ravaillac) and so cannot by themselves determine moral goodness; the criterion must be checked against the moral quality of ends, not merely formal fitness of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythms and moving equilibrium as moral criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's special theory that moral development is judged by 'rhythms' and a 'perfect state of moving equilibrium' (the law of change from homogeneous to heterogeneous and back).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer treats this as mechanical necessarianism; argues that if the universe merely moves through differentiations and integrations toward equilibration (and wreck), the theory is scarcely reconcilable with ordinary high-strain morality. The guidance is to beware mechanistic accounts that erase moral responsibility or meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for moral causation and free will (consciousness-based agency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral theory should acknowledge moral causation as given by consciousness and distinguish it from physical causation — i.e., it must account for what has been called 'free-will' (the difference given us by consciousness between moral and physical causation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer insists moral causation is the most certain and momentous fact of our being and that reducing moral causation to physical causation (automatism) is fallacious (example: Edwards' arguments leading to absurd ascription of crimes to an All-Good). A viable ethic must preserve moral agency as experienced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with ordinary moral sentiment and denunciations of wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must be reconcilable with ordinary moral sentiment — the passionate denunciation of wrong and the high strain of common moral feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer argues mechanistic necessarianism clashes with ordinary morality (e.g., indignation at atrocities). A theory that treats moral acts as mere evolutionary adjustments risks undermining moral censure and praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding justification of selfishness via 'struggle for existence'
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral system must not implicitly warrant selfish or predatory action by appealing to the 'struggle for existence' or survival-of-the-fittest metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer raises the objection that if 'adjustment of acts to ends' is the criterion, figures like Borgia or Bonaparte could claim moral goodness; the theory must answer why such well-adjusted evil acts are not morally good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical motivational force across social strata
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory ethic must produce motives effective for common people as well as for the educated — it must influence the masses whose conscientious performance of duty sustains society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer objects that Spencer's appeal to a distant future social state or evolutionary goal will not motivate those concerned with immediate survival or daily drudgery (examples: Bill Sykes, Glasgow bank director, William Tweed, the mass of common people). The guidance: test whether the theory gives accessible motives to ordinary lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of individuality and death
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should take account of individuality and death — the individual's finite life and hopes — rather than offering only abstract, long-term collective goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes ultra-evolutionary philosophers neglect individuality and death; a moral theory that ignores these facts risks being irrelevant to personal moral striving or consolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and historical accuracy (claims about origins of religion and ceremony)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a theory makes historical or anthropological claims (e.g., religion arising from cannibal chieftains, ceremony being primordial), those claims must be historically defensible and not speculative or 'unhistoric.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer challenges Spencer's adoption of Tylor's animism/cannibal-chieftain account and his thesis that ceremony is primordial; historical and philological evidence (Rig-Veda, Zendavesta, Hebrew scriptures) do not support such sweeping historical assertions. Guidance: avoid building ethical systems on unverified historical theses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to socioeconomic realities (labor, poverty, industrial conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral theory ought to be applicable and sensitive to the concrete conditions of most people's lives — drudgery, overwork, poverty — not only to a suburban or well-off individual's choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer points out Spencer's ideal man is a suburban villa proprietor and that such exemplars ignore the masses who must work to survive; test ethics for applicability amid real social hardships (miners, cab-drivers, farm-labourers, factory workers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of a practical, strong inducement or deterrent (societal stabilizer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should supply a basis of morality that will act as a strong inducement to right action and as a deterrent to wrong, capable of preventing a dangerous moral interregnum in society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer finds Spencer's system does not 'act as a strong inducement or deterrent' on the mass of mankind and so cannot be relied upon to save society from moral convulsions; the guidance is to evaluate whether a moral system can sustain societal moral order in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of quasi-religious faith in inevitable progress (evidential basis for optimism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory should not rest on requiring quasi-religious faith that all agencies of progress will continue unimpeded or that no new evils will emerge — optimistic predictions must have evidential support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer warns that belief in an 'evolutionary millennium' often requires faith that social and sanitary evils will vanish; the guidance is to ground hopeful social prognoses in evidence rather than mere assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and substantive contribution (does it provide a new basis of morality?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond eloquence and acute observation, a work of ethics should offer a genuinely new and practicable basis for morality, not merely rhetorical or interesting commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer concedes much that is 'acute, eloquent, interesting' in Spencer, but concludes the 'Data of Ethics' does not present 'a new basis of morality' nor a practical answer for motivating the masses; evalute whether the work advances the field materially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency between author's sentiments and theoretical implications
rubrics_metrics.description: An ethical system should not be internally inconsistent — the author's expressed moral sentiments must cohere with the logical consequences of their theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer points out Spencer's strong moral sentiment (protest against oppression) is inconsistent with a theory that makes moral attitudes mere products of evolutionary stages (e.g., bishops and militiamen 'could no more help' acting as they do); the guidance is to check for such contradictions.
